subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: The 2, 5 and 10 times tables
objectives: By the end, I can recall facts from the 2, 5 and 10 times tables.

vocabulary.definition: a family of multiplication facts that all use the same number
make groups of the same size and find the total
one multiplication you know by heart
say it fast, from memory, without counting

emphasize: A times table is just repeated skip-counting written as facts — five 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) IS 5 × 5.
Use the count or the array to FIND a fact, then aim to RECALL it from memory.
Keep commutativity alive: 2 × 10 = 10 × 2 — turning a fact around never changes the total.

keyConcepts: last-digit patterns: 2s are even, 5s end in 0 or 5, 10s end in 0
misconceptions: recalculating a turned-around fact from scratch instead of using commutativity
thinking tables are pure rote with no meaning — losing the skip-count and array that live inside each fact
hooks: Count five 5p coins — that's a times-table fact in disguise!

digital: animated number-line jumps with fact labels

video.title: The Counting by Fives Song | Counting Songs | Scratch Garden
video.watchTask: Sing along and count in 5s with the song. Every number you land on is a 5-times fact — when you hear 25, shout '5 × 5!'

afterCheck.question: Counting in fives, what comes after 20 — and which times-table fact is that?

plan.goal: Reveal that a coin count IS a times-table fact; retrieve equal groups from Lesson 9.
plan.note: The reveal — 'you just did a times-table fact in disguise' — is the hook. Don't teach yet.
plan.successCriteria: Child counts 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 along and says 3 × 5 means '3 groups of 5'.

script.say: Count these five 5p coins with me: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Guess what — you just did a times-table fact in disguise! Five 5s is 5 × 5 = 25. Today we collect these facts so they pop into your head super-fast. Quick memory check first: what does 3 × 5 mean?
script.adaptHints: Swap coins for the child's favourite collectible in packs of 5 (sticker packs, gems). Listen for '3 groups of 5'; if shaky, redraw a quick 3-by-5 array.

stuckProtocol: If '3 × 5' draws a blank: draw 3 rows of 5 dots — 'three groups of five — count them in fives: 5, 10, 15.'

plan.goal: Build the 5 times table from skip-counting, one jump per fact; show the patterns in the 2s and 10s.
plan.note: Each jump on the line gets its fact label — 'a fact is just the skip-count, frozen'. Then the shortcut patterns: 10s end in 0, 2s are the doubles.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees jumps of 5 labelled 1×5, 2×5, 3×5… and can say the pattern for the 10s (they all end in 0).

script.say: I'll build the 5 times table from skip-counting. Watch my jumps. One 5 is 5. Two 5s — 10. Three 5s — 15. Each jump is a brand-new fact: 1 × 5 = 5, 2 × 5 = 10, 3 × 5 = 15, 4 × 5 = 20, 5 × 5 = 25. A fact is just the skip-count, frozen! The 10s are even easier — they ALL end in 0: 10, 20, 30, 40. And the 2s? They're the doubles you already know: 2, 4, 6, 8. Find a fact by counting… then remember it, so next time it just pops out.
script.adaptHints: Say the skip-count rhythmically, like a chant. If the child joins in, let them lead the last two jumps.

plan.goal: Match facts to arrays and totals together; the child confirms each with a skip-count.
plan.note: The child does the matching; the character narrates the array ('4 rows of 5'). Confirm 4 × 5 on the count: 5, 10, 15, 20 — then jump tables: 'so what's 4 × 10?'
plan.successCriteria: Child matches the facts correctly and answers 4 × 5 = 20 and 4 × 10 = 40.

script.say: Let's match facts to their answers. Here's 4 × 5 — look at my array: 4 rows of 5 dots. Count the rows in fives with me: 5, 10, 15, 20. So 4 × 5 = 20. Now you match the rest — and here's the clever bit: once you know 4 × 5 = 20, what do you think 4 × 10 is? The jumps are twice as big!
script.adaptHints: Pause for each match. If the child counts every dot one by one, nudge: 'count a whole ROW at a time — 5, 10, 15…'

blocks.prompt: Match each fact to its total.

wrongAnswers.remedy: It's 4 GROUPS of 5, not 4 plus 5. Count the rows in fives: 5, 10, 15…

wrongAnswers.why: didn't notice the jump size doubled for the 10s
wrongAnswers.remedy: 4 × 10 is four jumps of TEN. Count them: 10, 20, 30…

plan.goal: Reveal whether the child uses commutativity and can recall (or quickly find) 5 × 5.
plan.note: The key diagnostic: does the child answer 10 × 2 instantly from 2 × 10, or start recalculating from scratch?
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 10 × 2 = 20 without recounting and gives 5 × 5 = 25 (recalled or found by skip-counting).

script.say: Quick-fire time! If 2 × 10 = 20… what is 10 × 2? … And one more: what is 5 × 5? After you answer, tell me — how could you CHECK 5 × 5 super-fast?
script.adaptHints: If the child answers 10 × 2 instantly, celebrate the shortcut by name: 'you turned the fact around — nothing to work out!'

options: You have to count it all again
blocks.explain: Turning a multiplication around never changes the total: 2 × 10 = 10 × 2 = 20. Picture the array rotating — same dots!

check.question: If 2 × 10 = 20, what is 10 × 2? And what is 5 × 5?
check.expectedAnswer: 20; and 25 (check 5 × 5 by counting in 5s five times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25)

wrongAnswers.why: not using commutativity — treats the turned fact as brand new
wrongAnswers.remedy: You already know 2 × 10! Turning it doesn't change the total — picture the array spinning round.
Five GROUPS of 5, not 5 plus 5 — skip-count them: 5, 10, 15…

plan.goal: Quick-fire recall across the 2s, 5s and 10s; find unknown facts by skip-counting, then try to remember them.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. For any fact the child can't recall, they FIND it on the number line, then the director re-asks the same fact a minute later to push it into memory. Finish with a beat-your-time round if secure.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 4+ mixed facts correctly, including one commutative pair, with at least two recalled instantly.

script.say: Practice time — let's make these facts pop! I'll fire questions, you fire back answers. If one won't pop out, no problem: we skip-count to FIND it, then trap it in your memory for next time. Ready? Let's see how fast you are!
script.adaptHints: Frame the speed round with the child's interests (football rapid-fire, rocket launch countdown). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'this fact isn't memorised yet — that's normal.'
Go concrete: skip-count along the number line all the way to it.
One hint: 'Start from a fact you DO know and jump on — 5 × 5 = 25, so 6 × 5 is one more jump.'
Re-ask a nearby easy fact, then return to this one.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child names a fact they now own; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led — the character listens. The named fact becomes tomorrow's warm-up starter.
plan.successCriteria: Child states at least one 2/5/10 fact from memory without counting.

script.say: Last job, champion: tell me ONE fact you can now say without any counting at all. … Yes! That fact is yours forever. You used the facts you already knew to jump to new ones — that's the smart way to learn tables, and it works for every table you'll ever meet.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: deriving from known facts, using the turn-around trick, skip-counting to check.

wrongAnswers.remedy: It's 2 GROUPS of 5. Jump twice on the line: 5… 10.
How many jumps of 5 do we need? Just two — count them.

hints: Two jumps of 5.
Skip-count: 5, then one more jump.

reteach.say: Let's see it: two coins, 5p each. Count: 5… 10. Two 5s make 10, so 2 × 5 = 10.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Each jump is a whole TEN. After 20, one more jump of ten lands on…?
It's 3 groups of 10, not 3 plus 10. Count the jumps: 10, 20…

hints: Every 10s answer ends in 0.
Three jumps of ten: 10, 20, then…?

reteach.say: The 10s table is the friendliest — it's just counting in tens with a 0 on the end. Three tens: 10, 20, 30. So 3 × 10 = 30.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Six GROUPS of 5 — skip-count them on your fingers: 5, 10, 15…
Count the jumps on your fingers — you need exactly six fives.

hints: You know 5 × 5 = 25 — jump ONE more five.
Count in 5s six times, one finger per jump.

reteach.say: Start from a fact you own: 5 × 5 = 25. Six 5s is just one more jump: 25… 30. So 6 × 5 = 30. Jumping on from a known fact beats counting from zero every time!

wrongAnswers.remedy: Four whole TENS — count them: 10, 20, 30…

wrongAnswers.why: pattern slip — stuck the 4 on twice
wrongAnswers.remedy: Skip-count four tens on your fingers: 10, 20, 30, 40. Where do you land?

hints: The 10s all end in 0.
Count four tens: 10, 20, 30…

reteach.say: Four ten-pence coins: 10, 20, 30, 40. Four tens make forty — and see the shortcut? 4 × 10 just puts a 0 after the 4.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Seven GROUPS of 2 — count in 2s: 2, 4, 6…

wrongAnswers.why: wrote the digits side by side
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're counting seven pairs, not gluing digits. Count: 2, 4, 6, 8…

hints: Count in 2s seven times — one finger per jump.
7 × 2 is double 7.

reteach.say: Seven pairs of socks! Count them in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Seven 2s make 14 — and that's exactly double 7.

block.prompt: Match each fact to its total.

wrongAnswers.remedy: The 5s end in 0 OR 5, and the jumps are small. Count seven 5s: 5, 10, 15…
Nine 2s is the doubles count, nine jumps: 2, 4, 6, 8… keep going!

hints: Check the pattern first: 10s end in 0, 2s are even.
If a fact won't pop out, skip-count to it.

reteach.say: Detective trick: look at the endings! 60 ends in 0 — that smells like a 10s fact. 35 ends in 5 — only the 5s do that. Match the patterns first, then check by skip-counting.

block.statement: You have to work out 10 × 2 separately, because it's a different fact from 2 × 10.
block.explain: Turning a fact around never changes the total — 2 × 10 and 10 × 2 are both 20. Picture the array rotating: same dots!

wrongAnswers.why: commutativity not yet trusted — recalculates every turned fact
wrongAnswers.remedy: Draw a 2-by-10 array and turn it on its side. Did any dots appear or vanish?

hints: Think of the array spinning round.
Same groups, same dots — does the total change?

reteach.say: Here's the free-facts trick: every fact you learn comes with its twin! 2 rows of 10 has 20 dots. Tip it over — now it's 10 rows of 2… still 20 dots. Learn 2 × 10 and you get 10 × 2 for free.

block.prompt: You know 5 × 5 = 25. Use it to find 6 × 5 — no counting from zero!

wrongAnswers.why: added 1 instead of one more group of 5
wrongAnswers.remedy: One more JUMP, not one more step — the jump is a whole 5.

wrongAnswers.why: doubled instead of adding one group
wrongAnswers.remedy: 6 × 5 is only ONE jump past 5 × 5. Start at 25 and jump once.

hints: 6 fives = 5 fives + one more five.
Start at 25. One jump of 5 lands on…?

reteach.say: This is the mathematician's ladder: stand on a fact you own and take one step. 5 × 5 = 25. One more five: 25 + 5 = 30. So 6 × 5 = 30. You never need to count from zero again!

block.title: Jump on from a known fact
steps: Start at the fact you know: 5 × 5 = 25

block.prompt: Could these numbers be answers in the 5 times table? Sort them!

wrongAnswers.why: saw a 5 in the number and ignored the last-digit rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: The rule looks at the LAST digit only. What does 54 end in?
Count in 5s past 20: 20, 25 — did you ever say 23?

hints: Look at the LAST digit only.
Counting in 5s you only ever land on numbers ending 0 or 5.

reteach.say: Say the 5s out loud and listen to the endings: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30… every single one ends in 0 or 5. That's the 5s' uniform! 23 ends in 3 — wrong uniform, so it can never be a 5s answer.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Nine whole TENS — that's a lot more than 19! Count: 10, 20, 30…
One zero, not two: 9 tens. Count in tens nine times and check where you land.

hints: Nine tens — the answer ends in 0.
Shortcut: 9 × 10 puts a 0 after the 9.

reteach.say: Count nine tens on your fingers: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90. Nine fingers, ninety! The shortcut — a 0 after the 9 — works because ten 9s and nine 10s are the same thing.

block.prompt: A friend says: 'I know 2 × 8 = 16, but 8 × 2 is too hard for me.' What would you tell them?
block.sample: 8 × 2 is the same fact turned around — it's 16 too. The array just rotates; no new work needed.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: 8 × 2 = 16 as well — turning a multiplication around never changes the total

wrongAnswers.answer: They need to count 8 twos from scratch
wrongAnswers.why: commutativity not applied — treats the twin fact as new work
wrongAnswers.remedy: Picture the 2-by-8 array tipping onto its side. Do any dots appear or disappear?

hints: What happens to an array when you turn it?
Every fact comes with a free twin.

reteach.say: Tell your friend the free-twin secret: 2 rows of 8 and 8 rows of 2 are the SAME 16 dots, just turned round. Knowing one means you already know the other — half the tables for free!

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave 2s, 5s and 10s randomly and add a beat-your-time round.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach, skip-count the fact on the number line together (CPA step down), then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 5+ correct across levels 2–3 including one commutative pair and one derived fact (e.g. 6 × 5 from 5 × 5), with at least two answered instantly → mastery ≥ 0.8 for '2/5/10 times-table recall'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'this fact isn't memorised yet' or 'the × turned into a + there'.
Drop a CPA stage: skip-count along the number line, or draw the array.
Give ONE hint: 'start from a fact you DO know and jump on.'
Re-ask a nearby easy fact, then return to the missed one.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Frame quick-fire rounds with the learner's interests (football rapid-fire, rocket countdown, coin collecting). Re-ask any fact the learner had to work out a minute later to convert it into recall. Never change the numbers.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with a fact the child can now recall instantly (drop a level if needed), then process praise: 'you jumped on from facts you knew and used the turn-around trick — that's how tables are really learned.'

differentiation.support: Keep the number line visible and skip-count aloud to every fact; stay on one table at a time (10s first — the friendliest); coin and array pictures on hand.
differentiation.stretch: 'Hit the Button' style speed round mixing all three tables; derive bigger facts (8 × 5, 9 × 10) from known ones and explain the jump.

extension: Beat-your-own-time tables challenge — record today's score on 10 mixed facts; next session, try to beat it.
assessmentEvidence: Child recalls a spread of 2/5/10 facts (finding the rest by skip-counting), including a commutative pair and one fact derived from a known one.
revisitLater: Daily 60-second tables round (2s, 5s, 10s). These facts power division (Lesson 11), the retrieval workout (Lesson 12), money (Unit 4) and fractions of quantities (Lesson 14).
